items.title: Developing pre-service teachers’ AI competence: a quasi-experimental study of a TICII-based methodical system
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education requires the purposeful development of pre-service teachers’ pedagogically grounded, responsible, and effective competence in using these technologies. Existing international frameworks (TPACK, DigCompEdu, the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers) provide a general basis for technological-pedagogical integration but do not fully operationalize the diagnostic, individualization, and ethical dimensions of AI competence as an integrated instructional and assessment system for teacher education. Methods This article reports a multi-institutional quasi-experimental study of a methodical system informed by the TICII (Transformation-Individualization-Competence-Inclusivity-Integration) conceptual model, conducted with master's-degree pre-service teachers in AI-related and computer-science fields across six higher education institutions in Uzbekistan over the 2023-2024, 2024-2025, and 2025-2026 academic years. The study examined the effect of a TICII-informed methodical intervention, supported by the EduAI platform, on pre-service teachers’ AI competence. A control group (n = 139) and an experimental group (n = 144) were compared at baseline and at the final stage using Pearson's chi-square (χ 2) test for competence-level distributions, treating this between-group comparison as the primary inferential analysis. Results The two groups did not differ significantly at baseline (χ 2 = 0.095, p = .954). At the final stage, a statistically significant difference was found between the groups (χ 2 = 31.124, p < .001, Cramér's V = 0.332). Descriptively, the proportion of experimental-group participants at the high level rose from 13.9% to 47.9%, compared with 15.1% to 20.1% in the control group. All statistical formulas applied are reported in full. Discussion The findings indicate that the TICII-informed methodical system was associated with substantially stronger development of pre-service teachers’ AI competence than conventional instruction.

items.title: Development and Validation of a Technology-Enhanced Distributed Collaborative Learning (TEDCL) Model for Hybrid Secondary Education
items.abstract: Although hybrid learning has expanded rapidly in secondary education, digital technologies are often used for content delivery rather than structured collaboration. This study developed and evaluated the Technology-Enhanced Distributed Collaborative Learning (TEDCL) model through an ADDIE-based Research and Development process and a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design. Participants were 50 Grade 7 and 8 students at Christian Junior High School Kali, Southeast of Minahasa, Indonesia; 25 received TEDCL-based instruction, and 25 received conventional technology-supported instruction. Ten teachers supported implementation, and three experts reviewed the model. Student engagement was measured with a Likert-scale questionnaire covering behavioral engagement, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, feedback availability, and learning motivation. Expert validation yielded an overall mean of 4.67/5.00 (SD = 0.49), and the questionnaire showed an overall Cronbach’s alpha of 0.91. Mean engagement increased from 3.90 to 4.42 in the experimental group (+0.52) and from 3.05 to 3.31 in the control group (+0.26). The reported unadjusted posttest comparison favored the experimental group, t(48) = 9.18, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 2.60. However, the groups differed at pretest, so the posttest contrast cannot by itself establish that TEDCL caused the observed difference. The findings support the model’s promise in this school context while indicating the need for baseline-adjusted analyses and replication with broader samples.

items.title: Digital Marketing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Applications, Consumer Impact and Ethical Challenges
items.abstract: Digital marketing has changed more in the last few years than in the previous two decades, and much of that change comes from artificial intelligence (AI). Brands now use machine learning, natural language processing and generative models to segment audiences, personalise messages, automate customer conversations and predict what people are likely to buy next. This paper examines how AI is being used in digital marketing, what benefits it brings to businesses and consumers, and what risks it creates. The study is descriptive and qualitative in design and relies on secondary data drawn from peer-reviewed journals, regulatory documents and published conceptual frameworks. Using a narrative literature review and a funnel-based analytical framework, the paper maps AI applications across the awareness, consideration, conversion and retention stages. The review finds that AI improves targeting accuracy, speed of content production, campaign efficiency and customer service availability, but that these gains depend heavily on data quality, human oversight and consumer trust. Concerns around privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency and over-automation remain unresolved. The paper concludes that AI works best as a partner to human marketers rather than a replacement, and it suggests directions for future empirical research, including primary studies in the Indian market.

items.title: Dissecting the effect of reward on naturalistic visual search: reward improves search efficiency more than it speeds within-fixation processing
items.abstract: Motivation powerfully shapes human performance, yet its effects on natural behavior are distributed across multiple perceptual, cognitive, and motor processes, making it difficult to isolate which changes drive behavioral gains. We examined how performance-contingent reward facilitates naturalistic visual search, asking whether it globally accelerates ongoing visual processing or qualitatively reorganizes search strategy. Participants performed a “Where’s Waldo?” search task while their eye-movements were monitored. They were assigned to either a reward group, which could receive a monetary reward for fast target detection, or a control group, which received no reward. As expected, reward substantially shortened search time. Eye-movement analyses revealed that rewarded participants searched more efficiently, showing less redundant sampling of previously inspected locations and more effective progression toward the target. The effects of reward changed over the course of the trial, with accelerated guidance toward the target early in the search and enhanced detection once the target was foveated later in the trial. Critically, decomposition of total search time quantified the contributions of these component changes to faster target detection in the reward group, and indicated that the reward-related advantage was driven predominantly by a more efficient reorganization of exploration rather than by uniformly shorter processing at each step. We conclude that reward does not merely speed up processing, but instead qualitatively reorganizes how observers sample, guide, and use visual information during complex behavior. By decomposing search into its constituent processes, this approach provides a framework for identifying how motivation shapes behavior across manipulations and populations.

items.title: Dissociable cognitive mechanisms of generative AI in education: evidence from CC-Eval, a standards-anchored benchmark for teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering educational workflows, yet educational research still lacks clear evidence on which functional cognitive components—rather than which brand names—drive success and failure when models assist teaching. Methods We introduce CC-Eval v1.0, a standards-anchored benchmark of 1,555 items spanning six equal-weight educational workflow tasks in Teaching Chinese to Speakers of Other Languages (TCSOL): grade knowledge (KNO), error diagnosis (ERR), essay scoring (SCO), teaching generation (GEN), culture/pragmatics (CUL), and standards/pedagogy (PED). Eleven free/light-tier large language models were evaluated under default application programming interface (API) settings, alongside a full second-judge pass over rubric-scored items. Results Equal-weight (macro) totals were only modest overall and were sharply dissociated by task: culture/pragmatics was consistently the strongest area; selected models reached comparatively usable scoring bands, yet with non-trivial predicted-mean bias; error diagnosis and grade knowledge remained weak; and level-controlled rewriting and textbook-standard clause locating showed systemic near-floor failure even when scenario drafting appeared fluent. A full second-judge pass over rubric-scored items yielded only moderate overall agreement, with a higher linear association on pedagogy rubrics than on open-ended culture pragmatics. Intertask correlations across the 11 models further suggest a breakdown of a unitary positive manifold, including negative covariances between scoring and constrained generation or error diagnosis. Discussion We read this fingerprint heuristically as a functional map of dissociable GenAI educational components-parametric standards memory, constraint satisfaction under graded input, evaluative score meaning, and pragmatic/cultural mediation-framed as properties of GenAI as an external cognitive prosthesis within a human-AI collaborative educational system, rather than as evidence of a unitary “AI teaching intelligence” or of an underlying cognitive architecture. The contribution is an education-facing, reproducible measurement map with cautious implications for how GenAI should be theorized, trusted, and scaffolded in standards-heavy language teaching.

items.title: Do ethics matter? Perceived ethics and students’ acceptance of generative AI in management education
items.abstract: This paper examines students' intentions to use generative AI (GAI) in higher education by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with the critical dimension of perceived ethics. Using two independent international samples from a global business experiential-learning project (Study 1, N = 3402; Study 2, N = 1586), comprising predominantly undergraduate and master's students from more than 80 reported home countries in each cohort, we tested the extended model. Approximately half of each sample reported prior academic GAI use. The results indicate that perceived ethics is positively associated with both attitude toward GAI and behavioral intention to use GAI in both studies. Prior GAI use moderated the relationship between perceived ethics and behavioral intention in Study 1, but this effect did not replicate in Study 2. The consistent direct relationships across the two independent samples support perceived ethics as a relevant extension of TAM for understanding students' acceptance of GAI in higher education. Theoretically, this suggests incorporating perceived ethics into technology-acceptance research, while practically it underscores the need for clear guidance on ethically appropriate GAI use in higher education.

items.title: El papel de la IA en la mejora de la inclusión de las personas con discapacidad en la industria turística
items.abstract: AI is playing a transformative role in enhancing the happiness of people with disabilities in the tourism industry by making travel more accessible and inclusive. By addressing physical and social barriers, AI provides equitable access to tourism, allowing disabled travelers to enjoy experiences with greater comfort and ease. Smart infrastructure and innovative solutions are creating an environment where accessibility needs are met, directly enhancing the overall satisfaction and happiness of disabled tourists. Key AI innovations like advanced navigation systems and accessible transportation enable individuals with disabilities to travel more independently, boosting their confidence and reducing the need for assistance. This autonomy contributes to a more fulfilling travel experience, allowing disabled travelers to explore destinations more freely and with less stress. AI-driven personalized services further enhance the experience by catering to the unique needs and preferences of each traveler, ensuring their specific requirements are met, which elevates their enjoyment and comfort. Additionally, assistive technologies such as speech recognition software and real-time translation devices simplify navigation in unfamiliar environments, reducing the anxiety associated with travel. These tools lead to smoother experiences and increased satisfaction. AI-powered data analysis also supports tourism operators by providing insights into the evolving needs of disabled travelers, allowing for continuous improvement of services. This ongoing refinement ensures that the tourism industry remains adaptable and inclusive, fostering greater happiness and promoting a more inclusive world for all travelers.

items.title: Emerging Developments in Wearable Technologies for Healthcare: A Semi‐Automated Horizon Scan
items.abstract: Horizon scanning is a foresight methodology that supports the early identification and assessment of emerging developments, trends, risks, and evidence gaps to inform research, policy, and decision‐making. This study aimed to advance horizon scanning methodologies for emerging health technologies by evaluating the use of large language models (LLMs) to support filtration and data extraction within a live horizon scan of literature, funding portals, clinical trials, and patents. Using wearable technologies as a case study, LLM‐assisted workflows were evaluated within a human‐in‐the‐loop framework. LLM‐assisted filtration achieved high sensitivity across data sources and reduced the volume of records requiring manual review, while semi‐automated and automated extraction demonstrated high sensitivity across most evaluated variables. An Acceptability Profile was used to assess automation performance in relation to decision criticality, risk tolerance, safeguards, and intended use. Together, the findings demonstrate that LLM‐assisted automation can support horizon scanning workflows with appropriate validation and human oversight. The live horizon scan identified differences between innovation activity and clinical validation across wearable technology applications, a predominance of consumer devices, and limited evidence in certain populations, including children. Patient and public involvement highlighted considerations relating to usability, acceptability, trust, and likely real‐world adoption. This study provides a practical and transparent approach for implementing automation in horizon scanning to support timely and actionable evidence generation.

items.title: Emotionally supportive pedagogies and student wellbeing: the role of teacher empathy, classroom belongingness, and classroom emotional climate
items.abstract: Introduction Empathic teaching may support student wellbeing, but its effects may depend on classroom emotional climate. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined classroom belongingness as a mediating pathway and positive emotional climate as a moderator. Methods Two studies with Chinese university students used a 2 × 2 between-subjects video experiment independently manipulating teacher empathy and classroom emotional climate. Study 1 (N = 160) assessed manipulation effectiveness and stimulus comparability. Study 2 (N = 428) measured anticipated classroom belongingness immediately after exposure and psychological wellbeing (WHO-5) approximately two weeks later. Data were analysed in R using confirmatory factor analysis and baseline-adjusted conditional process models with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Higher teacher empathy increased classroom belongingness under both climate conditions, with a larger effect under positive climate. Belongingness was positively associated with subsequent wellbeing. Conditional indirect effects were significant under both conditions and stronger under positive climate; the index of moderated mediation was 0.280 (95% bootstrap CI [0.065, 0.545]). Discussion Findings support a statistical indirect pathway from teacher empathy to subsequent wellbeing through anticipated classroom belongingness, strengthened by positive classroom emotional climate. Because the mediator was measured rather than experimentally manipulated, causal interpretation of the indirect effects is limited.

items.title: Employee Trust in Generative Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Corporate Social Responsibility Communication: Transparency, Human Oversight and Authenticity
items.abstract: This study investigates a framework integrating Stakeholder Theory, Signalling Theory, and Trust Theory to examine how CSR GenAI Disclosure Transparency (AIDT) and Perceived Human Oversight in GenAI‐Enabled CSR (PHO) are associated with Stakeholder Trust in GenAI‐Enabled CSR (ST). This study further investigates the statistical indirect associations through Stakeholder Empowerment Perception (SEP) and Perceived CSR Authenticity (PCSA). Data were collected from 330 respondents using a structured online survey administered through Prolific Academic and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings indicate that employees' perceptions of AI‐related CSR disclosure transparency and human oversight of GenAI‐enabled CSR were positively associated with stakeholder trust, both directly and indirectly through perceived stakeholder empowerment and CSR authenticity, respectively. This study contributes to responsible AI governance and GenAI‐enabled CSR communication research by identifying distinct indirect associations linking transparency with trust through empowerment and human oversight with trust through authenticity.

items.title: Empowering Socially Sustainable Mobility: How Intrinsic Motivations Shape the Intention to Adopt Intelligent Vehicle Automation Feature Sets for Diverse User Groups
items.abstract: The sustainable intention of using intelligent vehicles relies not only on technological advancement, but also on an explicit clarification of user intrinsic motivations. This study explores how cognitive, emotional, and behavioral empowerment shape drivers’ intentions to use intelligent vehicle automation features. Based on Delphi consultation and rigorous psychometric testing, we develop and validate a measurement scale and classify automated functions into three dimensions: smart interaction, vehicle control, and attention management. Using valid survey data from 614 drivers, the empirical results reveal that cognitive empowerment acts as the most powerful predictor of usage intention, surpassing the effects of emotional and behavioral empowerment. This study extends empowerment theory to human–vehicle interaction contexts and challenges the technology-dominated design paradigm that ignores user enablement. The findings provide user-centric design guidelines and policy references for fostering social and commercially sustainable intelligent mobility. However, we explicitly acknowledge that greater willingness to use automation features does not necessarily translate into realized environmental outcomes; linking feature engagement to broader social and commercial sustainability remains a critical avenue for future research.

items.title: Engaging university students with media theory through art-inspired creativity
items.abstract: The study investigates how creative activities including storyboarding, collaging, drawing, poetry writing, poster making, and basic cartography can engage students with abstract media concepts. Informed by Reeve and Tseng’s concept of ‘agentic engagement’ and Veiga et al.’s four-dimensional framework, and drawing on interviews with students and staff, the research explores how creativity, craftiness, and applied imagination can influence students’ engagement from a cognitive, behavioural, affective, and agentic perspective. The results, collected over a two-year period and examined through a dual-pronged approach, combining Thematic Analysis with Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis, indicate that creative pedagogies were commonly associated with students’ perceptions of their active contribution to the learning process, positioning creativity within an agentic dimension of engagement. The study demonstrates that creative affordances can enhance intellectual and active participation in class, and in supporting student learning. However, the implementation of creative activities may also face resistance among students, mostly due to self-consciousness and fear of judgement, which may inhibit spontaneous creative explorations. This article aims to spark a discussion over the benefits and challenges of using creativity to teach media concepts at university level, and to share tested ideas for whoever wishes to implement similar activities in their teaching.

items.title: Epistemic framing in AI-mediated university physics problem solving: a qualitative multiple-case study
items.abstract: Research on large language model-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in physics education has examined model performance, students’ evaluations of generated responses, and learning outcomes. Less is known about how generated explanations and calculations enter students’ observable physics problem-solving activity. This qualitative multiple-case study examines epistemic-frame sequences and their relation to solution quality, alongside students’ interactions with ChatGPT and their subsequent use of generated contributions. It analyses 30 submissions from 73 students across five university courses: 22 using ChatGPT and eight without it. ChatGPT was selected because its free version was students’ most frequently reported GenAI tool for independent study. Written artefacts and interaction records were analysed using Nguyen et al problem framing framework, with solution quality assessed independently. Activity recurrently moved between conceptual and algorithmic physics, but frame-sequence length did not distinguish solution quality. Challenges and reformulations made students’ evaluation of ChatGPT responses visible, whereas incorporation without documented evaluation sometimes carried generated errors into final submissions. The heterogeneous dataset confines interpretation to qualitative patterns and precludes causal comparison. The findings identify students’ observable evaluation and use of generated responses as a key link between GenAI output and documented physics reasoning.

items.title: Factors associated with teachers' adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Vietnamese high schools
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in high school History teaching remains underexamined. This study assessed associations among AI awareness (AAI), attitudes toward AI use (AAIU), technical support and resources (TSR), organizational culture and environment (OCE), practical application (PA), and teachers’ perceived impacts on students and learning outcomes (ISLO). An online survey yielded 335 responses from Vietnamese high school History teachers with prior AI-use experience; 17 incomplete or invalid cases were excluded, leaving 318 responses for partial least squares structural equation modeling. All eight prespecified direct paths were positive and statistically significant. The strongest associations were PA with ISLO (β = 0.599), AAI with AAIU (β = 0.597), and TSR with PA (β = 0.445). Significant specific indirect associations were also observed through AAIU, TSR, and PA. The model explained 66.2% of the variance in AAIU, 38.5% in TSR, 61.9% in PA, and 68.8% in ISLO. Because the data were single-source, self-reported, and cross-sectional, the results do not establish causality or objective student learning effects. The study provides a context-specific application of general AI-adoption constructs and highlights the relevance of teacher development, technical resources, and school-level support for responsible AI use in Vietnamese high school History teaching.

items.title: FigmaEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents in Professional UI Design
items.abstract: Recent advances in AI agents have enabled autonomous UI design using professional tools such as Figma, yet evaluating their design capabilities remains challenging due to the open-ended nature of design tasks and the absence of unique ground truths. We introduce FigmaEval, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on professional UI design tasks, comprising 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma design files. FigmaEval adopts a constrained-specification, open-solution paradigm, standardizing task requirements and design resources while allowing agents to independently determine layouts, visual hierarchies, component composition, and visual presentation. To assess design quality beyond reference similarity, we develop 22 expert-grounded evaluation rubrics across six dimensions and introduce a human evaluation arena where professional designers compare agent-generated designs through blinded pairwise judgments. Evaluating eleven models under a unified Figma agent setup, we find substantial agreement between rubric-based assessments and human preferences, alongside distinct differences in design practices and quality--efficiency trade-offs. FigmaEval provides a framework for systematically assessing professional UI design capabilities and understanding the strengths and limitations of current AI agents.

items.title: From AI Literacy to Employee Performance: A Systematic Review of Learning and Training Transfer
items.abstract: Effective workplace use of artificial intelligence (AI) requires employees to identify appropriate tasks, critically evaluate AI-generated outputs, and exercise professional judgment. However, the extent to which AI-related competencies acquired through training are transferred to everyday workplace practices and contribute to improved employee performance remains unclear. This systematic review examined how employee AI literacy was measured, developed through professional training, and associated with training transfer and job performance. Peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2019 and October 2026 were identified through searches conducted using two web search engines and supplementary reference screening. Methodological quality was assessed using the 2018 Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Given the heterogeneity of measurement approaches and research designs, the findings were synthesized thematically. The review included 43 empirical reports, of which 10 evaluated professional training programs. AI literacy was assessed using self-reported measures, objective knowledge tests, and proxy indicators derived from professional experience or employee profiles. Training programs commonly incorporated practical exercises, project-based learning, and reflective activities to develop AI-related competencies. Although several studies reported the application of acquired skills in workplace settings, evidence of sustained training transfer and long-term competency utilization remained limited. Variations in outcome measures and the predominance of nonrandomized research designs constrained the ability to establish whether AI literacy directly improved employee performance. Based on these findings, the review proposed a conceptual framework linking professional training, AI literacy development, training transfer, and job performance. Future research should empirically examine these relationships through longitudinal workplace assessments and independent, objective performance indicators, including task quality, task completion time, and error rates.

items.title: From Decision Support to Delegated Clinical Action: Governing the Autonomy Gradient of AI-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems
items.abstract: AI-driven clinical decision support systems can prepare executable orders, communicate with patients, and initiate multistep workflows, raising unresolved questions about delegated clinical authority. This viewpoint proposes a 5-level clinical autonomy gradient: informational support (A0), advisory decision support (A1), human-confirmed execution (A2), bounded delegated action (A3), and adaptive autonomous management (A4). Classification applies to a task-action pair within its deployment workflow. Execution authority and case-specific human authorization anchor assignment; decision influence, temporal reach, and scope adaptability describe the configuration. The action-enablement boundary (A1-A2) introduces executable action preparation requiring explicit, informed, case-specific authorization before release. The delegation boundary (A2-A3) permits execution without contemporaneous, case-specific authorization. We adapt an automation scope of practice to record permissions and operating conditions, and an autonomy safety case to link authority to deployment-specific evidence and residual risks. Proposed controls address effective human review, interacting systems, proportionate governance, and withholding, downgrading, or suspending actions when supporting conditions fail. Applications to documented systems and hypothetical scenarios illustrate classification reasoning without establishing reliability or delegated-action safety. Greater autonomy is optional; A1 or A2 may remain appropriate. Independent evaluation must assess classification agreement, feasibility, implementation burden, and effects on care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: From Language Teacher to Educational Developer: An Analytic Autoethnography of Human–AI Collaboration in English Language Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming educational practice, yet existing research has limited attention to how sustained human–AI collaboration reshapes teachers’ professional capabilities. This study employed analytic autoethnography to examine the professional journey of an English language teacher who collaborated with generative AI to design and develop multiple educational applications, including digital assessment systems, customised learning management system extensions, vocabulary learning tools, and AI-assisted language learning applications. Data consisted of reflective journals, AI interaction logs, development artefacts, and implementation records, which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal that authentic pedagogical problems initiated iterative cycles of human–AI collaboration and continued to the simultaneous development of technological and pedagogical capabilities that culminated in educational innovation and professional identity transformation. Based on these findings, the study proposes the Teacher Capability Transformation through Human–AI Collaboration (TCT-HAIC) Model, which conceptualises teacher capability development as a cyclical process driven by authentic educational challenges followed by sustained collaboration with AI. The study contributes a novel perspective by positioning generative AI not merely as an instructional tool but as a collaborative partner that expands teachers’ capabilities for continuous professional learning and educational innovation.

items.title: From naïve certainty to intellectual humility: how an AI-SSI curriculum reshapes high school students’ socioscientific orientations
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of an ENACT model-guided, Artificial Intelligence-related Socioscientific Issues (AI-SSI) curriculum on high school students’ socioscientific orientations (SO). While SSI-based pedagogy is recognized for enhancing scientific literacy and moral development, its specific effects within the domain of AI ethics remain underexplored. Employing a mixed-methods pretest-posttest design, this research investigated the influence of a 10-week AI-SSI intervention on 45 Chinese tenth-graders’ SO. Findings revealed significant pre-to-post declines in self-reported SO across all four dimensions --- ecological worldview, social and moral compassion, socioscientific accountability, and scientific evidence views. However, qualitative interview data suggest that these declines reflect epistemic development and the emergence of intellectual humility: students transitioned from simplistic, absolutist views toward more nuanced, conditional, and critical understandings of AI-SSI dilemmas. These findings imply that initial decreases in self-reported competencies may signal deeper epistemic development, including enhanced critical reasoning and more calibrated self-awareness of complexity. This study underscores the need for assessment strategies that can capture such intricate cognitive transformations. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-SSI instruction, when implemented under supportive conditions, has the potential to foster intellectual humility and nuanced ethical reasoning—dispositions that are important for navigating an AI-saturated world. These findings offer preliminary implications for AI-SSI, civic literacy, and responsible innovation.

items.title: From Replacement to Augmentation: A Human-Centered Framework for Consumer Robots
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and related hardware and software technologies have accelerated the development of consumer robots, creating new opportunities for robots to support people in everyday life. However, advanced technology is only the foundation for achieving this goal. A complete design concept for robots aimed at ordinary consumers is also needed. This paper examines the importance of positioning consumer robots as tools for human augmentation, the reason why consumer robot interaction design should mainly use intuitive operation, and the safety issues that influence user trust and acceptance. The analysis argues that consumer robots should prioritize human augmentation rather than complete robot autonomy. This approach protects consumer control while giving users stronger capabilities. In addition, robot products can only be psychologically accepted when consumers trust them. To achieve this positioning, intuitive interaction can reduce the barriers for ordinary consumers and allow more natural interaction. Products should also provide data privacy protection, control-right protection, and safety that can be perceived by users. The significance of this paper is that it provides a consumer-centered design framework for robots aimed at ordinary consumers.

items.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
items.abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

items.title: Generative AI Reliance, Developer Skill Atrophy, and Late-Stage Project Risk: A Mediation Analysis of Software Engineering Teams
items.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) coding assistants accelerate initial code generation, their downstream consequences for practitioner skill retention and software delivery stability remain underexplored. Drawing on cognitive load theory, automation bias theory, and technical debt theory, this study investigates how developer skill atrophy (DSA) mediates the relationship between generative AI reliance (GAIR) and late-stage project risk and technical defect escalation (LPR) across a sample of active software engineering practitioners (N = 142). Ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions and a 5,000-resample non-parametric bootstrap mediation model reveal a statistically significant competitive dual-path mechanism. Specifically, habitual reliance on GenAI strongly predicts developer skill atrophy (β* = .619, p < .001), which in turn strongly predicts late-stage project risk (β* = .672, p < .001). The indirect mediation pathway through skill atrophy is substantial and positive (a*b* = .502, 95% Boot CI [.338, .588], p < .001). Conversely, once skill atrophy is held constant, direct GenAI reliance exhibits a statistically significant protective effect against late-stage project risk (β* = -.228, p = .002), yielding a net positive total effect (c = .249, p = .025). Qualitative practitioner reflections (n = 48) corroborate these findings, highlighting superficial code reviews, degraded mental execution models, and late-sprint integration bottlenecks. These results resolve the productivity-versus-risk paradox of GenAI adoption and demonstrate that AI coding tools improve delivery reliability only when paired with deliberate verification and skill-retention practices. items.title: GENERATIVE AI-MEDIATED ORAL ENGLISH LEARNING IN TECHNICAL EDUCATION: EFFECTIVENESS, OPPORTUNITIES AND PEDAGOGICAL CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created new opportunities for oral English practice, but evidence specific to post-secondary technical education remains limited. This paper examines the effectiveness, instructional opportunities and pedagogical challenges reported in a bounded set of studies involving diploma and polytechnic learners. A structured scoping-review-informed search covered publications from 1January 2022 to 31 October 2026. Five accessible bibliographic exports yielded 4,007 rows, reduced to 3,756 records after preliminary deduplication. As the wider corpus was not fully screened, the evidence set was frozen on 1 November 2026. Three full-text-verified primary studies were synthesised, while one mixed-tool study was used for implementation context only. The strongest comparative study reported an overall posttest speaking advantage for the GenAI-supported group (Hedges’ g = 0.63, p = .003); however, only interaction remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Other studies described benefits for speaking-task preparation, dialogue practice and confidence, alongside mixed performance results, overreliance and methodological limitations. GenAI may therefore supplement teacher-guided oral English instruction, particularly when activities are linked to technical communication and followed by independent speaking tasks. The findings are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and do not establish a general causal effect on oral proficiency.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in English Language Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: This systematic literature review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being used in English language learning and what effects it has on students' language skills, motivation, and overall learning journey. GenAI refers to intelligent systems that can create written content, simulate conversations, and provide instant help to learners — tools that have become increasingly noticeable since 2020 as helpful resources for reading, writing, speaking, and vocabulary practice. While many people are excited about these technologies, research findings still show mixed results. There are ongoing concerns about how accurate the information is, whether learners might depend too heavily on AI, how it affects independent thinking skills, and what constitutes proper use. For this review, twenty-three research papers published between 2020 and 2026 were examined, using a thematic approach to bring together the key insights. Studies were selected based on how closely they relate to English teaching, the quality of their research methods, and whether they specifically looked at real GenAI applications in language learning. The results show that, generally, GenAI helps improve writing quality, builds speaking confidence, keeps learners more engaged, and makes practice opportunities more accessible. However, the evidence also leans heavily toward higher education and writing tasks, with less known about long-term results. Key challenges include the risk of over-reliance, possible impacts on critical thinking, and unequal access across different learner groups. This review concludes that GenAI has real potential to support language learning but it works best when used alongside clear teaching strategies and ethical guidelines. Based on these findings, recommendations suggest that schools and teachers create structured guidelines for responsible GenAI use, and that future research expands across more diverse educational settings to ensure these tools truly benefit all learners fairly.

items.title: Global Automation Atlas
items.abstract: Whether automation can replace or support workers depends not only on task content, but also on the conditions under which work is performed. Existing exposure measures typically assign fixed scores to tasks, capturing country differences only through employment structure. We use a large language model to classify 18,797 tasks in 124 economies by feasible exposure, labour substitution or augmentation, technology type and reliance on artificial intelligence. Accounting for country conditions changes occupation rankings and improves predictions of firms’ technology use. Exposure ranges from 3.3% to 61.6% of tasks and rises with income. Lower-income economies have fewer exposed tasks, but exposure is more concentrated in rule-based, labour-substituting automation, whereas labour-augmenting uses of artificial intelligence become more prominent with development. Women are disproportionately employed in occupations exposed to labour substitution. Model rationales for exposure more often mention machinery, digital records and connected systems, whereas rationales for non-exposure point to local knowledge and trusted relationships.

items.title: Governing LLM decision authority in tourism: A bounded generative agency framework for multi-stakeholder itinerary planning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support tourism itinerary decisions, yet factual grounding alone cannot establish whether a recommendation is acceptable to stakeholders or feasible to implement. This study develops SilverRoute, a framework integrating LLMs, geographic information systems (GIS), and multicriteria decision analysis. Under bounded generative agency, the LLM interprets needs and explains outcomes, while spatial evidence and formal rules govern feasibility, stakeholder acceptability, coordination, and recommendation or abstention. Evaluation used 4,750 facility and service features, 5,459 road features, and 698 cultural points of interest across 48 age-friendly tourism planning scenarios in Ya'an, China. An evidence-grounded LLM achieved 100% factual-claim accuracy but only 45.14% protocol alignment and recommended routes in all eight infeasible cases. Bounding its authority raised alignment to 100% and eliminated inappropriate and forced recommendations. In 40 recommendable scenarios, SilverRoute respected all stakeholder acceptability boundaries, whereas scalar baselines crossed at least one boundary in 17.5-20.0% of cases. Ablations showed that screening acceptability before aggregation provided most of the protection, while Nash bargaining became more consequential as preferences diverged. Time-boundary and repair tests showed that abstention can identify the requirement blocking action and support planner-confirmed adjustments without relaxing protected thresholds. The findings show how explicitly allocating decision rights can make itinerary planning auditable while supporting personalization and protecting stakeholder requirements.

items.title: Governing the next generation: a framework for the safe and equitable deployment of artificial intelligence, robotics, and immersive technologies in ophthalmology
items.abstract: Objective A new generation of technologies – artificial intelligence (AI), AI-guided surgical robotics, and immersive systems including virtual and augmented reality – are transforming ophthalmic practice across diagnoses, surgery, training, and patient engagement. Each domain has generated compelling clinical evidence; each has also exposed governance gaps – that, if unaddressed, risk entrenching inequalities, undermining patient safety, and erode clinical trust. This Mini Review synthesises the governance landscape across all three technology domains. Methods A narrative review of primary evidence, regulatory frameworks, and governance literature was conducted across AI diagnostics, AI-guided robotic surgery, and immersive technology platforms in ophthalmology, with a focus on publications between 2018 to 2026. Results Five cross-cutting governance failures common to all three domains are identified: dataset underrepresentation in training and validation; the absence of equity surveillance in post-deployment monitoring; an interpretability gap at the point of clinical use; an absent regulatory framework for agentic and continuously learning systems; and a lack of structured AI literacy in clinical training. Conclusion We propose a unified five-domain governance framework applicable across AI, robotics, and immersive technology in ophthalmology. Governance should not be a constraint on innovation – it should form the infrastructure on which innovation can be safely scaled.

items.title: Governing the Public-Sector Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Ghana: Data Sovereignty, Human Accountability and the Limits of Technical Oversight
items.abstract: This article contends that the decisive moment in the governance of public-sector artificial intelligence in Ghana is the moment of acquisition. A system’s deployment, audit, and later challenge all matter, but each is shaped by an earlier and far less visible choice: the tender document, the evaluation criteria, and the contract through which a public institution either retains or quietly surrenders its capacity to answer for the decisions the system will later inform. Ghana entered the final quarter of 2026 with a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched by the President on 24 April 2026, a Responsible AI Office announced but not yet shown to be operational, an Emerging Technologies Bill still under stakeholder review, and consultation drafts to replace the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and to amend the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), none of which has been enacted. The binding law governing the State’s acquisition of AI therefore remains the general law: the 1992 Constitution, Act 843, Act 1038, the Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772), and the Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663) as amended in 2016 and 2025, now supplemented by the Value for Money Office Act, 2026. Read together, these instruments impose meaningful obligations on public acquirers of AI, chiefly through articles 23 and 296 of the Constitution, the security and processor-contract duties in sections 28 to 31 of Act 843, the incident-reporting and critical information infrastructure regime of Act 1038, and the attribution and retention rules of Act 772. They also contain structural gaps which the procurement process is presently ill-equipped to close, namely a trade-secret limitation on the right to know the logic of automated decisions, an exclusion of decisions authorised by enactment from the automated-decision right, broad exemptions for national security, crime and taxation, and a procurement review system that grants standing to disappointed bidders but not to the citizens whose lives the purchased system will govern. The article develops a principle of non-delegable answerability and an Accountable Acquisition Framework of five conditions, distinguishes throughout between confirmed legal and policy requirements and proposed safeguards, and specifies the evidence that regulators, auditors, courts and researchers would need to evaluate implementation.

items.title: HCXAI-BR: A Reproducible Benchmark for Human-Centered Explainability and Contestability in Brazilian Health Information Guidance
items.abstract: Evaluating lay-facing health guidance from Large Language Models (LLMs) in the Global South requires human-centered explainability (HCXAI) tailored to local health systems and vulnerable populations. We introduce HCXAI-BR, a reproducible evaluation protocol featuring a five-axis, behaviorally anchored rubric—Safety, Accessible Language, Local Contextualization, Contestability, and Transparency—applied to 15 low-risk health scenarios in Brazilian Portuguese. In a pilot model-identity-masked evaluation of six global and national LLMs (90 responses), top-tier global proprietary and adapted commercial models achieved comparable performance (GPT-5.6 Luna 7.33/10, Sabiá-4 BR-SP 7.03/10, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 6.83/10), outperforming the national open-weight models, even on local contextualization within Brazil’s public health network (SUS/UBS). These pilot-scale comparisons, from fifteen prompts and a single response per model, demonstrate the protocol’s ability to discriminate between models, not a statistically validated ranking. An instrument-diagnostic pass resolved conceptual ambiguities between safety directives and epistemic humility, improving contestability inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.485). Our findings demonstrate that post-training alignment of capable base models offers a more viable path toward human-centered, sovereign AI in resource-constrained health ecosystems than small-scale pre-training from scratch. This single, confounded comparison (parameter count and training budget differ between the two models) should be read as a provisional, exploratory observation rather than a general, statistically established claim. items.title: How AI Dependence Influences Employees' Innovative Work Behavior: The Roles of Challenge-Hindrance Appraisals and Transactional Leadership
items.abstract: The extent to which employees rely on artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a new inflection point for organizational innovation. However, whether this “AI dependency” unleashes innovative potential or implicitly diminishes the willingness to innovate remains a subject of ongoing debate in academia. An analysis of data from 220 full-time employees reveals that AI dependency indirectly promotes innovative work behavior by stimulating challenge stress appraisals; simultaneously, it undermines employees' innovation input by exacerbating the perception of hindrance stressors. The findings offer micro-level evidence for understanding the psychological paradoxes in human-machine collaboration and extend the application boundaries of COR theory and the challenge-hindrance stress framework into the context of human-AI interaction. In practice, this study suggests that to truly unlock the innovation dividends of AI, merely introducing the technology is insufficient; organizations must also critically rethink management logic centered on transactional leadership.

items.title: Impact of a Peer Support Group Intervention on the Quality of Work Life of Medical Residents: A Quasi-experimental Study
items.abstract: Background and objective Medical residency involves substantial academic, clinical, and occupational demands that may affect physicians' well-being and quality of work life (QoWL). Peer support groups (PSGs) may provide structured opportunities for social support and collective reflection within this demanding occupational context. This study aimed to compare global QoWL between resident physicians who participated in a PSG intervention and those in a control group. Materials and methods A non-randomized, two-group quasi-experimental study included 117 resident physicians from a private tertiary-care hospital. Participants were sequentially allocated to an intervention group (n = 61) or to a control group (n = 56). The intervention consisted of six 60-minute weekly PSG sessions conducted in closed groups of 6-10 residents. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants with satisfactory global QoWL, assessed using the short version of the CVT-GOHISALO instrument. Its seven dimensions were evaluated as secondary measures, and mindful attention was assessed as a process-related characteristic using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS). Between-group comparisons were performed using the Pearson χ² test. Exploratory three-variable contingency tables based on Feinstein's simultaneous-effects framework were used to examine the primary outcome in relation to individual, clinical, occupational, and process-related characteristics. Results Satisfactory global QoWL was observed in 75.4% of the intervention group and 62.5% of the control group, corresponding to an absolute between-group difference of 12.9 percentage points. This difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.131). Among the secondary QoWL measures, the largest absolute between-group difference was observed for safety at work (65.6% vs. 50.0%; p = 0.088), although none of the dimensional comparisons reached statistical significance. Exploratory simultaneous-effects analyses showed heterogeneous intervention-outcome patterns across individual and occupational characteristics. Differences were descriptively larger among women and residents in critical-care services, whereas the pattern was attenuated or absent in some other strata. Workplace violence was associated with lower satisfactory QoWL in both study groups. Conclusions Resident physicians who participated in the PSG intervention showed a numerically higher proportion of satisfactory global QoWL than those in the control group, although the difference did not reach statistical significance. Exploratory analyses indicated that this pattern varied across individual and occupational contexts. PSGs may represent a complementary component of occupational-health strategies for medical residents, but further controlled studies with larger samples are needed to determine whether the observed patterns represent reproducible intervention effects.

items.title: Inclusive Design in Smart Healthcare
items.abstract: This chapter presents a literature review of research at the intersection of inclusive design, healthcare, and smart technologies. The study analyses peer-reviewed publications identified through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted search and screening process using the keywords “inclusive design”, “healthcare”, and “smart”. The aim is to identify dominant research themes and examine how user groups are represented in this body of literature. The results show that research is concentrated around smart and digital health technologies, healthcare environments, and conceptual design frameworks, with a strong focus on specific user categories such as older adults, people with disabilities, and patients with medical conditions. The findings highlight a tendency towards category-based approaches to inclusion, with limited consideration of broader and more complex forms of user diversity. The chapter contributes to the field by providing a structured overview of current research and by reflecting on the implications of user representation for inclusive design in smart healthcare.

items.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery in Public Senior Secondary Schools in Port Harcourt Metropolis.
items.abstract: This study investigated the influence of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery in public senior secondary schools in Port Harcourt Metropolis. Specifically, the study examined the influence of adaptive learning systems, chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading systems, and predictive analytics on teachers' instructional delivery. Three research objectives, three research questions, and three null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive research design was adopted. The target population comprised 1,866 teachers, from which a sample of 329 respondents was determined using Taro Yamane's formula. The multistage sampling technique was adopted for the sampling of the study. The instrument for data collection was a researcher’s designed questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence-Driven tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery. The instrument face and content was validated by three experts, one in Measurement and Evaluation and two in Educational Management in Rivers State University. The internal consistency of the instrument was determined using the cronbach Alpha statistics which yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.83. The data collected for the study was analyzed using mean and standard deviation for answer the research questions, while the null hypotheses were tested using independent sample t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that adaptive learning systems, chatbots, automated grading systems and predictive analytics influence teachers’ instructional delivery to a high extent, while intelligent tutoring systems influence teachers’ instructional delivery to a low extent. The hypotheses indicated no significant difference in the mean ratings of teachers in Port Harcourt City Local Government Areas and Obio/Akpor Local Government Areas on teachers’ instructional delivery. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that; school administrators provide teachers with continuous technical support on adaptive learning systems, and the Rivers State Ministry of Education should formulate clear chatbots policy guidelines and training for effective instructional delivery.

items.title: Innovative digital learning and teaching approaches for developing professional competence in nursing students: a scoping review
items.abstract: Innovative pedagogical approaches have emerged as potential solutions for promoting professional competence in the digital age, as technology integration into nursing education has highlighted the need for such strategies. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on innovative teaching and learning approaches used in nursing education and the professional competence outcomes, barriers, strategies and recommendations reported, with a view to informing future curriculum development. A literature search was conducted on 23 October 2026 in Web of Science, CINAHL, ERIC, PubMed and Scopus, covering articles published from January 2019 to the search date. Search terms were generic rather than technology-specific. Research questions and eligibility criteria were structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Results were synthesized inductively, reported outcomes were mapped to Miller’s pyramid of clinical competence, distinguishing objective from self-reported measures, and methodological quality was appraised with design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists. A total of 33 studies were included. Three main themes were identified: (1) Teaching methods, (2) Barriers and challenges of educational technologies and (3) Strategies and recommendations for advancing nursing education. The approaches fell into five categories; all four studies of tools supported by artificial intelligence were published in 2025 or 2026. Objective assessments supported placements at “Knows” in 20 studies, “Knows how” in three and “Shows how” in 17; six studies had no objectively assessed competence outcome. No study reported outcomes at the highest level of Miller’s pyramid (“Does”). Within the studies retrieved, simulation and virtual reality were investigated most often, and objectively assessed gains were reported mainly for performance under controlled conditions; transfer to independent clinical practice was not evaluated. Findings for game-based approaches were mixed, and mobile learning was most often associated with knowledge and observed skill performance. Confidence in the reported benefits is limited by heterogeneous designs, variable methodological quality, reliance on self-report at the “Knows how” level and outcomes measured mostly within two weeks of the interventions. The map is not exhaustive, and comparative, longitudinal evaluations are needed before the relative value of these approaches can be judged.

items.title: Internalising externalities through global technologies: an information systems–based extension of RBV and CBV
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to advance strategic management theory by proposing iRBV – an Information Systems-based extension of the resource-based view (RBV) and capability-based view (CBV). This essay argues that globally available technologies fundamentally change the role of firm resources and capabilities, enabling firms not merely to respond to market conditions but to reshape the rules by which markets operate. Drawing on RBV and CBV, the author proposes iRBV as a framework for understanding how firms can adopt and adapt global technologies – such as artificial intelligence and blockchain – to internalise externalities and create new markets. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a viewpoint on how firms can proactively reshape their environment by incorporating externalities into their strategies. The author proposes iRBV – an information systems (IS)-based extension of the RBV, CBV and natural RBV – as a theoretical advancement that enables management scholars and practitioners to develop business models capable of addressing market externalities, including climate change, at the firm level. Findings Through two illustrative cases – ChatGPT and the Libra coin – this essay demonstrates how global technologies can enable firms to reshape markets and internalise externalities that lie beyond the scope of traditional RBV and CBV. Climate change mitigation is presented as one significant application of this mechanism. Research limitations/implications iRBV is presented as a theoretical provocation rather than a fully operationalised framework. Its primary limitation is the reliance on illustrative cases rather than systematic empirical evidence. Future research should develop the microfoundations of iRBV – specifically the routines, heuristics and higher-order capabilities that enable firms to adopt and adapt globally available technologies for externality internalisation. Additional boundary conditions require investigation, including the applicability of iRBV beyond digital technologies, the role of power asymmetries and path dependencies in capability activation and the conditions under which profit-maximisation logic aligns with – rather than diverges from – the internalisation of societal externalities. Practical implications iRBV equips managers with a theoretical lens for identifying externalities as strategic opportunities rather than regulatory obligations. Firms with strong IS capabilities – such as those already deploying artificial intelligence (AI) or blockchain – are well positioned to develop business models that internalise externalities while generating profit. iRBV encourages managers to incorporate a global view of their strategic environment into firm strategy, treating the internalisation of externalities not as a cost of doing business but as a potential source of market dominance. Social implications iRBV suggests that addressing societal externalities – including climate change – need not depend solely on top-down regulation or international agreements. By providing firms with a profit-driven mechanism for internalising externalities, iRBV enables a bottom-up approach in which individual firms take the lead in reshaping market rules and addressing global challenges. This shifts the locus of responsibility from governments and international bodies to firms themselves, driven by intrinsic strategic logic rather than external mandate. If widely adopted, iRBV could contribute to a broader transformation in how business and society relate to one another in the face of global challenges. Originality/value This paper advances RBV and CBV into iRBV, a theoretical extension that positions globally available technologies as levers for internalising market externalities through intrinsic, profit-driven firm strategies. Illustrative examples demonstrate how technologies such as blockchain and AI could enable firms to address climate change – including CO2 traceability, cryptocurrency-based climate incentives and environmentally-linked search restrictions – while simultaneously achieving market dominance.

items.title: Is it true that Generative AI is Shaping Employee Identity and Working Practices to Become More "Digital"?
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing contemporary workplaces by influencing not only task execution but also employees’ understandings of professional competence, roles, and identity. This article explores how employees experience and negotiate changes in work practices and professional identity as GenAI becomes integrated into everyday work. Using an exploratory qualitative and interpretive approach, the study frames GenAI adoption, work-practice transformation, identity negotiation, and human–AI collaboration as interrelated analytical dimensions. The analysis indicates that GenAI can shift work from direct task execution toward task orchestration, in which employees formulate instructions, assess and revise AI outputs, and retain responsibility for final decisions. The resulting identity change is not automatic or uniform: employees may come to view themselves as AI-augmented professionals while also negotiating boundaries around expertise, autonomy, accountability, and meaningful work. GenAI can support efficiency and access to knowledge, yet it may also create dependence, intensified work expectations, and uncertainty about the value of human expertise. The article therefore conceptualizes digital employee identity as a negotiated and potentially hybrid professional identity rather than a simple consequence of technology use. These insights extend discussion of strategic human resource management by highlighting the importance of AI literacy, continuous learning, responsible AI governance, and human-centered work design. The conclusions should be interpreted in light of the exploratory design and the need for further empirical investigation across organizational and occupational contexts.

items.title: Just Because You Can, Does Not Mean You (Always) Should: The Ethical Implications of Using Generative AI in Chemistry Education
items.abstract: The proliferation of accessible generative AI platforms continues to accelerate in society. With this growth, educators are looking to understand how to best train their students to engage in their work and society with this new technology. Most research in this realm has focused on training students to consider when and how to use generative AI, with newer work focused on the impacts on learning. Yet, there has been little exploration of training educators and educational researchers on when and how to use generative AI. While there are some nascent ethical codes emerging, individual exploration of whether, when, and how to use AI in our role as educators deserves attention. In this manuscript, we describe three frameworks of normative ethics, namely, utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics, and explore instructor use cases for generative AI. We do not intend this work to advocate for a specific stance on the use of AI but to invite the reader and our community to engage with the question of their own ethical stance in the context of their own use of the new technology.

items.title: Large-scale clinical application of human-AI collaborative quality improvement program for prenatal ultrasound in an underdeveloped region of China: a quasi-experimental study
items.abstract: To evaluate whether human-AI collaborative models were associated with greater improvements in prenatal ultrasound quality compared with a purely-AI model in an underdeveloped region. We deployed an AI-based quality control system at county-level hospitals in Jiangxi, China, collecting ultrasound images covering 23 planes from mid-to-late trimester prenatal ultrasound screening from January to December 2024. The system scored each image (0-100) and classified it as standard (≥ 80) or non-standard (< 80). Three quality control models—purely-AI, theoretical training alongside AI (T-A), and hybrid human-led alongside AI (H-A)—were allocated at the prefecture-level city (non-randomized). A difference-in-differences framework was used to estimate the associations of the H-A and T-A models compared with the purely-AI group. Parallel trend tests were performed to assess the parallel trends assumption. A total of 131,024 images taken by 192 sonographers across 67 hospitals were collected. All three groups showed significant pre-to-post improvements in both standardisation and missing rates (all P < 0.001). The improvement in standardisation rate was 21.5% (95% CI: 20.7–22.3) for H-A, 19.6% (18.1–21.1) for T-A, and 19.3% (18.4–20.2) for purely-AI. Compared with the purely-AI group, the H-A group was associated with an absolute improvement of 2.2% (95% CI: 1.0–3.4; adjusted OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.22–1.93; P < 0.001), whereas the T-A group showed no significant additional benefit: 0.3% (95% CI: −1.4 to 2.0; adjusted OR: 1.14, 95% CI: 0.79–1.66; P = 0.479). In exploratory subgroup analyses, the H-A group showed potential additional benefits in specific subgroups. The H-A model was associated with a modest additional improvement compared with the purely-AI model in this underdeveloped region. These findings suggest that AI-based QC may serve as a foundational component, while the hybrid human-led intervention, though promising, requires further validation in outcome-linked studies.

items.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
items.abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

items.title: Learner agency and academic engagement in AI-supported higher education: The roles of e-learning autonomy and self-efficacy
items.abstract: The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to university students raises important questions regarding learners’ responsibility for their work and sustained engagement when assistance is easily accessible. This study investigated the relationships among e-learning autonomy, learning self-efficacy, and academic engagement within an AI-supported higher education environment. A cross-sectional online survey of 223 undergraduate students employed adapted measures to assess perceived capacity for self-directed learning, confidence in personal abilities, and participation in academic activities without excessive dependence on AI assistance. Regression-based mediation analysis indicated that e-learning autonomy was positively associated with both learning self-efficacy and academic engagement. Learning self-efficacy was also positively associated with engagement and showed a significant positive indirect association between autonomy and engagement, alongside a significant direct association. These results highlight autonomy and self-efficacy as interconnected learner resources linked to academic engagement in contexts where AI assistance is present. The findings advance understanding of the human dimensions of AI-supported higher education and underscore the need for institutions to address both AI access and the cultivation of students’ ownership of learning and confidence in their abilities.

items.title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

items.title: Learning Motivation in the Digital Age: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends and Emerging Themes
items.abstract: Objective: This study maps the development of research on learning motivation in the digital era from 2015 to 2025, focusing on publication trends, research contributions, theoretical foundations, and emerging research themes. Theoretical framework: This study identifies Self-Determination Theory as the main intellectual foundation, with Social Cognitive Theory as a supporting theoretical perspective developed separately. Literature review: The study includes literature on learning motivation in digital learning, especially intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, learning engagement, self-concept, and digital literacy. Methods: The study used bibliometric analysis of 190 open-access journal articles indexed by Scopus for the period 2015–2025 through Biblioshiny, including performance analysis, co-citation, keyword co-emergence, thematic mapping, and factorial analysis. Results: Publications increased by an average of 28.47% per year, with Indonesia, China, and Taiwan as the main contributors. The themes of learning engagement, self-concept, and digital literacy began to develop, while intrinsic and extrinsic motivation showed a declining trend. Implications: This study encourages the development of more diverse theoretical perspectives, the integration of the concept of self-efficacy, the use of longitudinal design, as well as the expansion of studies in the context of school education and Islamic religious education. Novelty: This study presents a mapping of the development of digital learning motivation before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, while also revealing the dominance of one theoretical foundation and identifying the direction of further research.

items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore how users leverage tools based on large language models (LLMs) to self-manage psychological well-being. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on affordance theory, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 participants and analyzed their use of ChatGPT for psychological well-being using grounded theory techniques. Findings Users learned about ChatGPT's potential through external influences, experimentation, and prior experiences. As their understanding evolved, they actualized various affordances but also encountered barriers when repurposing the tool for psychological well-being. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded account of how individuals appropriate a general-purpose LLM for psychological well-being. It identifies context-specific patterns for further affordance research and proposes user-informed design guidelines for LLM-enabled chatbots.
